Pregnancy often improves rheumatoid arthritis symptoms for many women, with estimates that about three-quarters to 70–80% of patients experience improvement during pregnancy [d7,d1,d6]. However, improvement is not universal; more than half of RA patients still have active disease during pregnancy in some studies, and about a quarter may have persistent or worsening symptoms [d5,d6,d7]. Mechanistically, hormonal shifts during pregnancy are thought to contribute to reduced disease activity, while postpartum hormonal changes are associated with flares [d4,d9,d8]. Differences in reported improvement rates reflect varying definitions and study methods rather than conflicting outcomes [d4,d2].
